Deloitte cuts 170 jobs in Australia, but it’s hiring 500+ elsewhere. Here’s why. 

Deloitte Australia is making about 170 roles redundant, roughly 2% of its ~11,000 non-partner workforce. At the same time, it plans to hire 500+ people for its outsourcing division.

This looks less like a simple cost-cutting story and more like a strategic pivot.

What’s behind it? 

- The $1B target: Deloitte wants to triple its managed services (outsourcing) business to $1 billion in revenue by 2030.

- Shifting client demand: Deloitte says it acted where there has been a “sustained shift in client demand.” Advisory and deals work has been under pressure, while tax, legal and technology work has grown.

- The search for steady revenue: Outsourcing means running back-office functions like finance on long-term contracts. It’s predictable, recurring income, unlike project-based consulting.

- Lower-cost delivery: These services are delivered by a mix of Australian teams and hubs in India.

It’s an industry-wide trend. The Big Four are all moving the same way: 

- PwC Australia is targeting $500M+ in outsourcing revenue by 2030 
- EY Australia already runs a ~$400M-a-year outsourcing business

My takeaway: 

The consulting model is changing. Clients want ongoing, outcome-based services over one-off advisory projects, and AI is pushing firms to rethink which roles they need.

Who builds your software: AI or the professional engineer?

The question itself is wrong. The common mistake is choosing between them; the correct move is distributing the roles.

In our plan for building our sales management system, we adopted the hybrid model:

AI builds inside a governed ecosystem against a written specification, while the professional engineer works as the quality line, not the production line: architecture review, execution governance, signing off every phase before delivery, and solving the technical knots AI can't untie.

Three direct results:

1. Cost drops, because you no longer pay for hours of execution — you pay for hours of technical judgment.

2. Intellectual property stays inside your own ecosystem, so no one becomes "essential enough to hold you hostage."

3. The excellent engineer stays, because professionals grow bored of executing and thrive on supervising — a smarter role raises retention.

The governing rule: the specification is a contract for both parties. Whoever builds — machine or human — works against written acceptance criteria, and whoever approves signs before delivery. This turns hiring from a gamble on a personal relationship into measurable architecture.

AI didn't make engineers cheaper. It made the best engineers more valuable.

Did you ever kick yourself for hiring someone who interviewed brilliantly but turned out mediocre on the job?

Andreessen Horowitz just posted a list of hiring tips, and 2 resonate with me in particular – but implementing them isn’t always straightforward.

Here’s the approach I’ve developed over the past decade to simulate practical work with candidates real-time during interviews.

First, avoid theoretical questions. Not: "how would you build a go-to-market plan?" - which invites a textbook answer and management speak.

Instead, get dirty: share a real-life scenario from your team and ask them to sketch a work artefact on a digital whiteboard while you give feedback. How good are they at putting ideas in writing in real-time? Do they accept redirection graciously or get defensive?

Business development roles - have them draft a short term sheet with specific commercials and ballpark pricing. Not a theoretical high-level outline. Ask them to spell out an important contract clause verbatim.

Account management roles - roleplay a difficult client. Can they stay empathetic and firm at the same time, and adjust as you feed them new information?

Product roles – provide an ambiguous scenario and ask them to build an AI prototype on screen-share with key flows and example pricing. Can they triage your signals into what matters vs. noise, and create something practical & realistic?

The pattern you’ll see is that weak executors might be fine outlining concepts, but stumble when it comes to the gory details. The clear red flag is the candidate who hesitates to dive into the little things, struggles to improvise, and retreats to describing how they "would" do it rather than actually trying to do it on the spot.

The one thing your practical interview still can't test is whether someone will sustain momentum: consistent follow-through over weeks, or persistence when things get hard. That's where references have a key place, especially unsolicited ones. They're not always objective or easy to get, but they're indispensable.

I highly recommend spending half your interview time on hands-on scenarios - your decisions will get sharply better. Some candidates are surprised at first ("you want me to come up with an actual marketing headline right now??"), but I’ve found that the strong ones really enjoy it. It gives them a concrete feel for the job that awaits.

775 new companies set up in DIFC in just the first quarter of 2026, up from 478 a year earlier.
 
If you are one of them, the clock started the day you signed.
 
The first 90 days of a new fintech or financial firm in DIFC decide how fast you can launch. And almost every item on the checklist comes back to one thing: people.
 
Here is how we see it.
 
Days 1-30: Get the foundation right
 → Key leadership and the regulated roles the regulator expects to see in place, such as compliance and MLRO
 → Your first core hires: the people who can speak with confidence to the regulator, banks and partners
 → A clear view of the skills you need now, and the ones you can add later
 
Days 31-60: Build the engine
 → Engineering, cloud, data and security talent to build and run your platform
 → AI and automation skills for onboarding, monitoring and risk
 → A hiring plan that does not stop for every new requirement
 
Days 61-90: Get ready to launch
 → Operations, risk and client-facing teams, in place before go-live
 → A governed way to bring in contract and project talent as demand shifts
 → Enough depth that one resignation does not become a launch delay
 
The pattern we see: regulated and senior roles are the hardest to fill, and the cost of a gap is a delayed launch.

For firms in the UAE, we start with the talent in the UAE first, and go for a global search only when the skill you need requires it. Buying AI is a lot like hiring someone. You can read the CV, sit through the interview and watch a great demo, but you don’t really know how they’ll perform until they’re doing the actual work. By then you’ve already hired them.

We see this everywhere in AI enterprise deployments. The demo goes well and everyone in the room agrees it looks useful. Then nobody wants to sign off on a full rollout based on a demo - it's just too risky

During my IIM days, the summer internship was the best hiring tool around. A highly motivated student worked closely with the team for two or three months, and if the work was good, they left with a final offer. Both sides knew exactly what they were getting.

Outside campus, that model is hard to copy. It’s expensive, it takes months and it doesn’t scale. And if the person left a year later, everything you’d put into them left too.

That's one of the beautiful advantages of AI - A deployment can run the same exercise in weeks. Training, integration, going live and scaling up all happen inside the pilot, so the client is judging real work instead of a demo. Unlike an intern, it doesn’t leave and take the training with it. We now run all our pilots this way, with one narrow use case and one clear way to measure it.

The chart below is a great example. In June, one client started a pilot with us on a single, narrow use case. It proved what it needed to, and they signed an annual contract in August. Usage has more than doubled since the contract, and October is on pace for 2.5x June.

Running pilots this way has given us very strong signals. Customers are more satisfied because they’ve already seen it work. The success metrics are agreed before anything goes live. And by the time a contract is signed, the whole organisation is clear on what the AI is doing and why.

Most founders think scaling an engineering firm to 6 departments requires hiring 20 people. 
We took the opposite bet at Botmartz AI Solutions.

Over the past month, we architected a private, local AI Operating System (AIOS) to run all 6 departments of our business—orchestrated by local open-weight models via Ollama, agentic state machines, and standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) drivers.

Here is what the architecture looks like under the hood:

🏢 The 6 Autonomous Departments:
1. Executive Command (Strategic decomposition & priority alignment)
2. Engineering & Research Labs (Autonomous code review & test suite benchmarking)
3. Growth & Generative SEO (Search Console indexing, Lighthouse audits & GEO citations)
4. Sales & B2B Proposals (Inbound lead qualification & custom pilot scoping)
5. Social & Community (Curriculum intake & cross-platform distribution)
6. Operations & Legal (Contract reconciliation & commit auditing)

🔌 The Unified Hardware / MCP Driver Bus:
Instead of fragile, bespoke API glue, our agents interact through standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers:
• ClickUp  for bi-directional project board and task synchronization
• GitHub for commit auditing and branch management across 180+ repositories
• WhatsApp Business via local Baileys bridge for incoming client triage
• Google Search Console & Google Lighthouse for continuous Core Web Vitals audits
• Google Antigravity to dispatch specialized subagents on isolated tasks

🧠 Local Privacy & Sovereignty:

By executing local open weights through Ollama, proprietary client datasets, internal task logs, and code refactoring loops never leave our private infrastructure.

The result? A 2-person core engineering team operating with the structured output, speed, and precision of a 25-person organization.

We are entering the era of the sovereign, AI-native enterprise. It’s no longer about whether an LLM can generate text—it’s about whether you can architect the system that orchestrates deterministic workflows.

When we started Jimmy, almost every client wanted their engineers on-site.

Remote wasn't anyone’s first choice. Trust came from being in the room.

We bet on remote anyway. Central and Western Europe didn’t have enough senior engineers, and we believed the best people didn’t need to sit in the same building to do great work.

We were grateful when Ondřej Kofroň from EAG gave our Eastern Europe-based team a chance. That first “yes” meant more than he probably knows.
Then COVID hit, and remote went from exception to default almost overnight.
But working remotely and hiring remotely are two different things. Cross-border contracts, payroll, compliance, and vetting someone you’ve never met in person are still where a lot of companies get stuck.

When the war in Ukraine started, we had to rebuild how we hire and how our team is structured. Today our engineers sit across the UK, Southern Europe, CEE, the Middle East, India and Pakistan.

We can cover all time zone requirements and help companies build the most skillful team without local market limitations.

The right AI or data engineer for your team probably doesn’t live in your city. Our job is to find them, vet them technically, and handle everything else so they can focus on the work.

What’s the hardest part of building a distributed team for you: finding the right people, or everything that comes after?

One thing I've deliberately let go of in the last 90 days: the idea that an interim executive is one person.

For most of my career, hiring an interim meant hiring a head. You got their experience, their frameworks and their network, for the length of the contract.

I don't bring my own AI agents into assignments yet. Data protection decides where and how that's possible, and it should. But I've stopped thinking of the next interim, me included, as one person. Research, analysis, the first draft of a board pack – more and more of that will arrive with the interim as tools, not as slides. You'll hire one person and get a small team.

For a CEO or a chair hiring an interim, that changes the interview. Ask what they work with, not only what they've done, and what happens to your data when they use it. The CV tells you about the person. The tools tell you how much of the work will still be running after the contract ends.

Which also means letting go of something less comfortable: a few frameworks I was quite proud of.

Planning to hire an AI development company?

Before signing the contract, ask these 5 questions. 🚨

Many AI projects start with an impressive demo. The more important question is what happens when real customers begin using the product.

Here is what I would ask:

1️⃣ How will you measure AI accuracy?
Ask how outputs will be evaluated, how realistic test cases will be created, and how failures will be identified.

2️⃣ How will you protect our data?
Discuss access controls, data retention, third-party AI providers, privacy requirements and security responsibilities.

3️⃣ How will the AI integrate with our existing systems?
Understand how it will work with your CRM, ERP, HRMS, databases or other business applications.

4️⃣ Who owns the source code and intellectual property?
Make ownership, repository access, documentation, third-party components and handover obligations clear in the agreement.

5️⃣ What happens when the AI makes a mistake?
Ask about human review, fallback workflows, monitoring, incident handling and ongoing improvements.

One more thing: don't evaluate a development partner only by the quality of its presentation.
Ask to see working software. Review its testing approach. Understand how progress will be measured.

At Xonier Technologies, we believe good software partnerships require transparency, clear ownership and measurable delivery milestones.

🔥 The best Teachers and School Leaders in the UAE and KSA are rarely found by an Algorithm or a Job Advert

A Head of Secondary resigns in February. You post the role, hundreds of applications arrive, and weeks later your HR department is inundated and no closer to the finding person you need.

🏫 In the UAE and KSA, where competition for strong educators is intense, AI screening and open advertising might be cheaper than Search but they're often the wrong tools for the roles that matter most. You get what you pay for.

🔎 In our experience the best people aren’t looking. Outstanding teachers and leaders are settled and performing. They respond to a confidential, considered conversation, not a job board. Advertising only reaches those actively searching. Search firms like EdSolut reach everyone else.

💯 As we all well know, volume isn’t quality. AI can sort CVs, but it can’t judge whether an “outstanding” school was outstanding in a comparable context, or whether someone has genuinely led change. It can also quietly screen out good candidates because it lacks flexibility of thought and insight.

🌏 The region isn’t a generic market. Licensing and attestation rules vary by emirate and by country. Curriculum fit matters, from British and IB to American and Saudi national programmes. Emiratisation, Saudisation and Vision 2030 all shape who schools need. Specialist recruiters, like us, live in this detail every day.

🌏 Regional uncertainty raises the stakes. Many UAE schools report staffing has held up better than feared, but recruiters describe overseas candidates delaying decisions, shorter hiring seasons and tougher competition for teachers already in-country. Candidates want candid, current advice on safety, contracts and contingency planning, and offers need to be held through to arrival. That is human work, and an advert or an algorithm can’t do it.

💯 Retention is the real cost. A weak hire can mean relocation spend, disruption to pupils and lower staff morale. A good search partner is accountable for long-term fit through rigorous referencing, honest conversations about life in the region and settling-in support.

Confidentiality matters. A retained search keeps the process discreet.

🤖 None of this means AI or advertising has no place. Both work well for high-volume, lower-risk roles. But for senior leaders and hard-to-fill specialists, human judgement and trusted relationships still make the difference.

💰 The question isn’t “what’s the cheapest way to fill this vacancy?” It’s “who will still be making a difference here in three years?”

The contract says independent. The daily instructions may say otherwise.
That gap matters when a Dutch company hires zzp.

Bouwend Nederland reports that on 18 October the Dutch tax authority reminded businesses of the 9 criteria for assessing zzp hiring. This is separate from the rate threshold discussed earlier: the question is how work is organised, not just the hourly price.

Before: ask AI to rewrite the contract so the hire looks independent. The wording changes; the work may not.

After: we compare daily practice with the 9 criteria. We record who makes decisions during the job, not just what the agreement says.

Example: an installation firm books a zzp specialist. The firm agrees when the specialist can enter the site. Once work starts, does the specialist plan the tasks, or does a manager assign them as the day unfolds? Neither answer alone determines status.

Clients and contractors may disagree about where independence ends. Do your site notes show who assigned tasks during the job?

For deliberate false self-employment, fines can reach 100%.

Wall Street just told AI agents: you can look, but you can’t touch.

JPMorgan, Schwab, and Citi all made the same call this month. Outside AI agents can read account data, but they can’t move money. Schwab’s CEO said his firm blocks attempts tens of times a week, and Jamie Dimon warned about rogue agents, possibly thousands of them.

That’s the banking answer to agent risk: read-only, full stop.

Web3 builders are exploring the opposite design: let the agent act, but inside hard limits. Spending caps, allow-lists of approved contracts, permissions that expire on their own. Same fear, different philosophy.

For hiring, that makes one profile unusually valuable: engineers who can design permission systems for software that holds value. Smart contract security, account abstraction, wallet infrastructure, plus a real understanding of how agents fail.

If you’ve built scoped permissions or session-key logic, lead with it.

We’re speaking with teams hiring for exactly this. Reach out if that’s you.

Perfect ratings do not answer every hiring question.

An excellent rating can offer useful context without answering the buyer's particular question. They may still need to know whether you have solved a similar problem, understand the constraints and can run the work reliably. Relevance gives general praise a place in the decision. Show the details that connect your history to the current assignment.

A five-star review about a small illustration commission may not explain suitability for a complex product launch. Look for relevant examples and discuss the proposed process. The rating remains useful context, but the new assignment still needs its own evaluation.

1. Select examples close to the client's need.
2. Explain the situation and your contribution.
3. Describe the process the buyer can expect.
4. Use ratings alongside concrete evidence and clear terms.

Build trust around the actual decision being made. A strong overall score should support that evaluation rather than replace it.

The lessons of corporate. 
when organizations face extreme, survival like replacing departments with AI agents—corporate branding like "Great Place to Work" or "Equal Opportunity Employer" often reveals itself to be corporate marketing rather than a safety net.
When a company must cut 30% of its workforce because AI agents can handle the workload, the transition is rarely a pure, objective meritocracy. In high-stakes corporate shifts, the workplace can absolutely feel like a "cowboy zone" where survival depends on internal politics.
Here is a breakdown of why this disconnect happens and how the internal power dynamics actually play out during an AI restructuring:

1. The Myth of the "Clean Slate" External Hire
When a company creates a new, highly coveted AI-native department, outsiders assume the company will post the job publicly and hire the best resume. In reality, leadership almost always defaults to internal allocation first for several survivalist reasons:
$Context over Credentials: Someone who already understands the company's messiest internal data, legacy political factions, and client quirks is highly valuable. They can train the AI agents much faster than a brilliant external prompt engineer who doesn't know where the company's "bodies are buried."
$Risk Mitigation: Hiring externally is a gamble. Moving an internal, trusted political ally into a powerful new AI role protects the executive's own fiefdom.

2. The Illusion of Corporate "Tags" and Certifications
Certifications like Great Place to Work or Equal Opportunity statements are heavily structured compliance frameworks and employer branding tools.
$These awards are largely based on employee sentiment surveys taken during stable times, heavily pushed by HR departments to attract talent. They do not dictate how a board of directors or an executive team will act when a disruptive technology threatens their quarterly profit margins.
$The Reality of "Equal Opportunity": This ensures that the process of hiring and firing follows strict legal guidelines to avoid discrimination lawsuits based on protected classes (race, gender, age, etc.). 
$Fiefdom Building: Managers who control the data pipelines or the budget will position their own loyalists as the "Supervisors" of the new AI tools to ensure their own departments don't lose funding or relevance.
$The "Savior" Narrative: Politically savvy workers position themselves as the bridge between the old world and the new world. They make sure the executives know they are the ones keeping the automated system from crashing.
$Nepotism and Protectionism: When roles contract, executives protect their inner circle. The "middle layer" of average, quiet performers who simply do their jobs without playing the political game are often the most exposed to layoffs

The Takeaway
The corporate messaging paints a picture of an orderly, fair meritocracy, but massive technological disruptions expose the raw, political core of corporate survival.
